client: I've been having a really hard time since my dad passed away a few weeks ago. I keep trying to sit down and focus at work, but my mind just goes blank or I end up staring at the screen for an hour without doing anything. And there's this weird mix of sadness and something that feels like anger underneath it all, which honestly confuses me and makes me wonder if talking to someone can even untangle any of this.
therapist: What you're carrying right now is incredibly heavy, and I want you to know that the confusion you're feeling — that mix of sadness and anger — is actually a very normal, human response to losing someone you love, not a sign that something is wrong with you. The way you're speaking, soft yet with a kind of urgency underneath, tells me there's a lot swirling inside that you're trying to hold together, and it makes complete sense that your mind is struggling to focus when it's quietly processing something this profound. Talking this through absolutely can help — grief rarely travels in a straight line, and we can work together to gently make sense of what all these feelings are telling you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly... part of me wonders if talking about it really does anything, or if it just keeps me stuck in it longer. Like, every time I start to think I'm okay, I'll catch myself reaching for my phone to text him, and then it hits me all over again that he's gone. I don't know if I want to keep poking at that wound.
therapist: That moment of reaching for your phone to text him — and then the wave of realizing he's gone — is one of the most quietly devastating parts of grief, and I hear how exhausting it is to keep getting pulled back into that pain. Your hesitation about talking makes complete sense; it's not resistance, it's actually a really understandable way of protecting yourself from something that hurts deeply. What I'd gently offer is that we don't have to poke at the wound — instead, we can work toward helping you carry it in a way that feels less like it's ambushing you when you least expect it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate that you're not trying to make me just "get over it" or whatever, because I've had people say that and it honestly just makes me feel worse. But I'm not sure I understand what you mean by carrying it differently — like, how do you actually do that? Because right now it just feels like grief is something that happens to me, not something I have any control over.
therapist: The way you're asking that question — softly, but genuinely wanting to understand — tells me you're already doing something important: you're looking for a sense of agency in something that has felt completely out of your hands. "Carrying it differently" doesn't mean controlling the grief or stopping those moments like reaching for your phone — it means gradually building a little more space around them, so that when they hit, you have some ground to stand on rather than feeling swept away. In CBT terms, we'd work on gently noticing the thoughts that come with those waves — like what your mind tells you in that moment — and slowly finding ways to respond to them that feel a little less like drowning.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That image of having "ground to stand on" actually resonates with me a little, because right now it really does feel like I'm just getting swept under every time it hits. But I'm not sure I trust myself to notice the thoughts in those moments — it all happens so fast, like one second I'm fine and the next I'm already three minutes into scrolling through old photos and feeling terrible. I guess I'm wondering if I'm even capable of slowing that down enough to actually catch what my mind is doing.
therapist: The fact that you're speaking with such openness right now, even while doubting yourself, actually tells me you have more capacity for this than you're giving yourself credit for. That spiral — fine one second, deep in old photos the next — feels instantaneous, but with practice we can start to find the tiny moments *before* the wave fully takes you, and those moments are where your ground gets built. You don't have to be perfect at catching it; even noticing *after* the fact, "oh, that happened again," is a real and valid first step.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, but it also feels a little too... optimistic, I guess. Like, when I'm in that spiral, there's no tiny moment I can grab onto — it just swallows me whole before I even realize what's happening. And honestly, the "noticing after the fact" thing kind of just makes me feel worse, like I'm tallying up all the times I failed to stop it.
therapist: You're pushing back on my framing, and I'm really glad you did — because you're right that if "noticing" is turning into a scorecard of failures, then it's not helping, it's just adding another layer of pain onto an already heavy load. Your voice carries something that sounds like genuine weariness with ideas that sound good in theory but don't quite land in the reality of what you're living through, and I want to honor that rather than keep handing you tools that feel like they don't fit. So let's set aside the noticing for now — instead, I'm curious: is there anything, even something small or seemingly unrelated to grief, that has ever given you even a brief moment of feeling like yourself again?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate that she's not pushing the noticing thing anymore, because honestly it was starting to feel like one more thing I was doing wrong. When she asks about feeling like myself again... I have to sit with that for a second, because it's a strange question. There was this one evening a few weeks ago when I was cooking — just something simple, pasta — and for maybe ten minutes I wasn't thinking about losing my mom, I was just... there, stirring the pot, and it felt almost okay.
therapist: That moment at the stove — just you, the pasta, the stirring — that's not a small thing, that's actually really significant, and I want you to hold onto it for a second rather than brush past it. Your words carry a quiet flicker of something almost like relief when you describe it, even as your voice sounds like someone who's been running hard and is still a little breathless from everything. That ten minutes wasn't you escaping your grief or failing it — it was a genuine glimpse of the ground we were talking about, and it came not from trying to manage your thoughts, but just from being absorbed in something simple and real.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess you're right that I didn't really think of it as anything meaningful at the time, I just... needed to eat, you know? But hearing you describe it that way makes me feel a little strange, like maybe I've been dismissing these tiny moments as nothing when they might actually be something. I'm just not sure I trust that feeling yet, because it seems too simple, like it can't really be enough when everything else still feels so heavy.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, almost tentatively, like you're holding something fragile — tells me that what you just recognized feels both true and a little frightening to trust. You don't have to trust it fully yet; that's completely okay. But I'd gently challenge the idea that something has to be big or dramatic to count — grief is so heavy precisely because it's made of all the small things, which means healing can also live in the small things, like a pot of pasta on a quiet evening.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that makes sense, what you're saying about the small things... but part of me still feels like if I let myself believe that a quiet evening alone with pasta counts as something good, I'm just lowering the bar for myself, you know? Like I'm settling for a life that's smaller than what I thought it would be. And that feels less like healing and more like giving up.
therapist: The way you just said that — quick, almost like you needed to get it out before you could second-guess it — tells me this fear of "settling" is something that's been sitting with you for a while, maybe even before your loss. That's a really important distinction worth gently examining: there's a difference between lowering the bar and simply meeting yourself where you are right now, in the middle of one of the hardest seasons a person can go through. Finding meaning in a quiet evening isn't giving up on a bigger life — it might actually be how you stay intact enough to find your way back to it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but there's this nagging voice that says if I get too comfortable with the quiet evenings, I'll just... stay there. Like, what if finding meaning in small things is just a really convincing way of giving up without admitting it to myself? I guess I'm scared that grief has already shrunk my world so much, and I don't want to accidentally help it shrink further by calling it "self-compassion."
therapist: The fear you're describing — that self-compassion might secretly be a trap — is actually a sign of someone who cares deeply about their own life and doesn't want to lose it, and that's worth naming because it's the opposite of giving up. Your voice is soft and careful right now, like someone trying very hard to think something through honestly, and I want to reflect back that the very fact you're *scared* of shrinking tells me there's a part of you actively fighting against it. Small moments aren't the destination — they're how you stay strong enough to want more.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but I also keep wondering if that "part of me fighting against it" is just exhaustion talking, not actual strength. Like, what if I'm scared of shrinking simply because I don't know what else to be, not because I genuinely want something more for myself? It feels important to be honest about that distinction, even if I can't fully figure it out right now.
therapist: The honesty in what you just said — spoken so softly, almost like you're confessing something you've been afraid to admit — is itself a form of strength, even if it doesn't feel that way right now. You're right that exhaustion and strength can look identical from the inside, and I don't want to paper over that with reassurance; but I'd gently offer that someone who is *only* exhausted usually stops asking these kinds of questions, and you haven't stopped. The fact that you're holding that distinction carefully, even when you can't resolve it, tells me there's something in you that still wants to understand itself — and that matters.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
